## Question 1 (4 points)

For each of the following scenarios, decide which continuous distribution would be most appropriate to use.

- This distribution is used to model variables for which all outcomes of that variable are equally likely. [Uniform]{style="color: red;"}

- This distribution would be used to model proportions, for example the proportion of time spent on a task out of the total time spent on multiple tasks. [Beta]{style="color: red;"}

- This distribution would be used to model the total time it takes for a given number of events to occur when times between events are exponentially distributed. [Gamma]{style="color: red;"}

- This distribution is often used to model the time until a single event occurs. [Exponential]{style="color: red;"}

## Question 2 (3 points)

You are measuring the time that passes between residential fires in a city where times between fires are exponentially distributed. Specifically, you are measuring the time that passes before 20 fires occur. If you know that 4 fires occur every day, then what is the expected length of time that passes before 20 fires occur (in days)?

[This is a Gamma random variable with shape $\alpha = 20$ and rate $\lambda = 4$. Then since $\text{E}[X] = \frac{\alpha}{\lambda}$ we have:]{style="color: red;"}

$$
\text{E}[X] = \frac{20}{4} = 5
$$

## Question 3 (3 points)

You know that wait times for buses at a particular bus stop are exponentially distributed and that 2 buses come every hour. In the code block below, compute the density of the wait time distribution at $x=1$ and $x=2$, $f_X(1;\lambda)$ and $f_X(2;\lambda)$ respectively.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
lambda <- 2

fdens_1 <- dexp(1, lambda)
fdens_2 <- dexp(2, lambda)

cat("f_X(1;2) and f_X(2;2) are", fdens_1, "and", fdens_2, "respectively")
```

Based on the answers you obtained above, are you more likely to observe wait times close to 1 hour or wait times close to 2 hours?

[The density around 1 is larger than the density around 2 so you would expect to see wait times closer to 1 hour than you would 2 hours.]{style="color: red;"}

## Question 4 (3 points)

You and your friend are standing in two different lines at an amusement park. You know that 4 people get to the front of each line every minute. You are currently the 20th person in your line and your friend is the 16th person in their line. What is the probability that you get to the front of your line before your friend gets to the front of theirs? Use the code block below to compute this probability.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
alpha <- 20
beta <- 16

prob_short_wait <- pbeta(0.5, alpha, beta)

cat("The probability you have a shorter wait time is:", prob_short_wait)
```
